subject: chemistry
question_text: What is entropy? Explain with an example.

verification.note: Unit 6 Thermodynamics is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.73-75), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book attaches ΔS(total) = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings) to 'any isolated system'; this card states it for any process, since an isolated system exchanges nothing with its surroundings. NOTE: the book also asks entropy at VSAQ 4a as one of three definitions in a bundle; that bundle is a separate card (ts_ipe_c1_td_define_entropy_terms), not a cut of this one, because its two other definitions cannot come from this step list. steps.label: Definition
lines: Entropy S is a measure of the randomness or
It is a state function and an extensive
The greater the disorder, the greater the
steps.why: Entropy turns disorder from a word into a measurable quantity, and being a state function makes ΔS depend only on the initial and final states.
common_mistakes: Calling entropy a form of energy — its unit J K⁻¹ shows it is heat divided by temperature, not heat.
steps.memory_tip: S for scatter: the more the particles are scattered, the larger S.
steps.margin_note: Disorder, state function, extensive — three checked words.

steps.label: Example
lines: When ice melts, the ordered crystal becomes
a liquid whose molecules move about freely:
steps.why: The question says explain with an example, so one concrete change (ice to water) plus the general ordering of the three states is the expected content.
common_mistakes: Writing the ordering backwards — the gas is the most disordered, so it has the highest entropy.
steps.memory_tip: Solid, liquid, gas: order decreases and entropy increases in that sequence.
steps.margin_note: One concrete example plus the S(g) > S(l) > S(s) line.

steps.label: Quantitative form
lines: For a reversible change at temperature T:
Units of ΔS: J K⁻¹ (per mole, J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
steps.why: The same quantity of heat produces a larger entropy change in a cold system than in a hot one, so the entropy change is the heat divided by the temperature at which it is transferred. Check the units from the formula itself: q(rev) in joules divided by T in kelvin gives J K⁻¹. The per-mole form J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ applies when q(rev) is the heat for one mole, which is how tabulated entropy values are quoted.
common_mistakes: Multiplying instead of dividing by T.
Writing the unit as J mol⁻¹, dropping the K⁻¹. Entropy is measured in J K⁻¹ and molar entropy in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
steps.memory_tip: Heat over temperature: q on top, T below, units J K⁻¹.
steps.margin_note: The reversible q and the unit both matter here.

steps.label: Spontaneity link
lines: A spontaneous process increases the total:
steps.why: Spontaneity is judged by the total entropy, not the system's alone. The book writes this sum for an isolated system; an isolated system exchanges nothing, so the sharper statement is system plus surroundings for any process.
common_mistakes: Testing spontaneity with ΔS(system) alone — freezing water lowers the system's entropy yet is spontaneous below 0 °C.
steps.memory_tip: Always add the two entropy changes: system plus surroundings, then check the sign.
steps.margin_note: Box the criterion; it connects this answer to the second law.

insider_note: The word explain moves this beyond the two-mark definition: the example, the formula ΔS = q(rev)/T and the total-entropy criterion each carry a mark of their own.
